newsitem.title: USA: Investors may turn to smaller issues, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Investors may turn to smaller issues, analysts say.

text.p: After a record-setting week on Wall Street, when stocks got a big boost from news on the economy and the balanced budget deal, investors may turn to smaller stocks that have lagged behind the overall market.
Analysts said that last week's rally finally began to extend beyond the small group of big-name stocks that have driven the Dow Jones industrial average near record highs.
The search for value appears to be moving into new territory.
"A lot of investors feel that the only areas with reasonable value are small- and mid-cap issues and some cyclicals," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.
"The reason is the full exploitation of those stocks which figure prominently in the indexes and the sense that it is a folly to chase them at these levels."

The stock market rounded out a strong week with the Dow jumping 94.72 points to 7,071.20 on Friday - within 14 points of its record 7,085.16 set on March 11. For the week, the Dow gained 332.33 points, a record.

The move in companies with smaller market capitalisation, so-called small- and mid-cap stocks that have languished during the market's long rally, was welcome since it would broaden the previously narrow rally, analysts said.

Through Friday, the Dow industrials were up 9.7 percent for the year but the Nasdaq composite index of high-technology and smaller stocks had gained just 1.1 percent while the Russell 2000 index of small stocks had fallen 2.4 percent.
The numbers include impressive gains by the two smaller-cap indexes on Friday.
Wall Street could get some further fuel from investor enthusiasm for a deal on a framework for a balanced budget by 2002, announced by President Clinton and the Republican-led Congress late Friday.

"This is something that (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan has wanted for a long time and has said would help keep interest rates down," said Anthony O'Bryan, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
Analysts said there could be some profit taking in big cap stocks this week.

"The market is overpriced," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "We could see a decline in large cap stock indexes such as the Dow and the S&P 500 but an improving relative performance by smaller cap issues as measured by the Russell 2000."
But worries about another rise in short-term interest rates when Fed policy-makers meet on May 20 should abate this week, some analysts said.

"The economic numbers (last week) relieved some of the urgency in the Fed's need to raise interest rates quickly, although they don't eliminate the risk of another rate increase," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter.

Canelo said the economy was strong enough to absorb more rate increases, and he believes the market may be overly concerned that another rise in rates would slow the economy, and corporate earnings growth, too much.
"Some people believe that a quarter point rise would slow the economy, but I don't buy that," he said. "A quarter point is meaningless from a corporate point of view, it's not relevant."
He said that the economy could "live with one or two rate increases but three or four more monetary tightening would be a different story."
Fed policy-makers raised short-term rates a quarter point on March 25 in a bid to ward off inflation. It was the first increase in more than two years.
